extracted.intended_audience: trademark practitioners, applicants, and parties litigating concurrent use proceedings before the TTAB
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluative standards for instituting, conducting, settling, and deciding concurrent use proceedings before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board, including proof of entitlement to registration, trial/briefing schedules, conversion from oppositions/cancellations, and effects of abandonment or settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement to concurrent registration (burden of proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: The concurrent use applicant has the burden of proving its entitlement to the registration(s) sought; the issue before the Board is the applicant's entitlement and the extent, if any, to which other involved applications or registrations should be restricted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if other parties default or a settlement excludes parties, each concurrent use applicant must prove entitlement as against every party to the proceeding that is not included in the agreement. The Board considers territorial use and likelihood of confusion when determining entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte showing to prove entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: A concurrent use applicant may, in some cases (e.g., after default by other users), prove entitlement by making an ex parte showing rather than through formal adversary procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte showings permit use of less formal procedures such as declarations or affidavit evidence instead of depositions or oral examinations. Such a showing usually suffices if the applicant can address many of the factors the Board considers in settlement agreements (see TBMP § 1110). If the ex parte showing is insufficient, judgment is entered against the concurrent use applicant, the proceeding is dissolved, and registration is refused.

rubrics_metrics.name: General conduct of concurrent use proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurrent use proceedings are conducted in the same general manner as oppositions or cancellations, except inter alia there is no complaint and the 'answer' is not the usual answer and is not always required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties are subject to disclosure and conferencing obligations. While many practices (discovery conferences, disclosures, discovery, motions, evidence, briefing, oral hearings, review) mirror oppositions/cancellations, the Board structures testimony periods and briefing to account for multiple plaintiffs/defendants in concurrent use cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failure to answer / default judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: If an answer, when required, is not filed, default judgment is entered against the non-answering party, precluding that party from claiming any right more extensive than that acknowledged in the involved concurrent use application(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even upon default, each concurrent use applicant still bears the burden of proving entitlement to registration. In certain default situations, the Board may allow an ex parte showing of entitlement; if an applicant fails to make a sufficient ex parte showing, judgment is entered against it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accelerated Case Resolution (ACR) and expedited determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may obtain expedited determination of concurrent use proceedings by stipulating to Accelerated Case Resolution (ACR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concurrent use applicants are even more likely to achieve expedited determination by means of informal ex parte-type showings after default. See TBMP §§ 528.05(a)(2) and 702.04 for ACR procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of offering evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The order in which parties offer evidence depends on whether they own an involved application or registration and, when multiple applicants own involved applications, on the filing dates of those applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two or more parties own involved concurrent use applications, the party with the latest filing date goes last; testimony periods are scheduled so each plaintiff presents its case in chief against each defendant, each defendant presents its case and meets each plaintiff, and plaintiffs have rebuttal periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial and briefing schedule structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board sets discovery conference deadlines, disclosure dates, discovery opening/closing dates, testimony periods (separated by 60-day intervals), pretrial disclosure deadlines, and briefing periods structured for multiple parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony periods are separated from discovery and each other by 60-day intervals with intervening pretrial disclosure deadlines. Briefing periods are scheduled so that each plaintiff files a main brief, each defendant files a main brief meeting each plaintiff's brief, and plaintiffs may file reply briefs. The Board issues an order with specific dates upon instituting the proceeding. (Sample schedules provided.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement agreements must negate likelihood of confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board will not enter judgment finding concurrent use applicant entitled to registration based on a settlement agreement unless the terms of the agreement are sufficient to persuade the Board that confusion, mistake, or deception is not likely to result from continued concurrent use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the settlement agreement is insufficiently persuasive, the Board generally will suspend proceedings and allow submission of a revised agreement correcting deficiencies. Agreements 'worked out by the parties in good faith' are considered; 'naked' consent agreements lacking measures to avoid confusion are not persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical provisions to include in concurrent use settlement agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Settlement agreements commonly include mutually exclusive geographic territories and may include additional provisions to prevent confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of additional provisions: (1) agreement not to use or advertise in the other's geographic area; (2) steps necessary to prevent actual confusion; (3) establishment of a 'buffer zone' between territories; (4) recitation of specific differences between marks and goods; (5) information on particular aspects of goods, services, or channels of trade that preclude confusion; (6) agreement to use distinct packaging/labeling/signs; (7) information as to length and extent of concurrent use and whether any actual confusion has occurred. These factors are not all-inclusive; parties may include other relevant facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet advertising and geographic scope concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet advertising increases geographic scope of advertising and may affect likelihood of confusion, but measures can reduce possibility of consumer confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of mitigating measures: a statement on each party's website that it is not affiliated with other parties; a website statement indicating the party's specific geographic area of use; displaying the subject mark on the website in close association with another mark or trade name or in a certain form. Even with internet advertising, entitlement may still be shown (see CDS Inc. v. I.C.E.D. Management Inc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of settlement excluding some parties
rubrics_metrics.description: If a settlement agreement does not include every party to the proceeding, each concurrent use applicant still has the burden of proving entitlement to registration as against every party not included in the agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A default judgment for failure to answer against a non-included party does not relieve an applicant of the burden to prove entitlement as to that party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of abandonment of an involved application
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant whose application is the subject of the concurrent use proceeding abandons its application without the written consent of each adverse party, judgment will be entered against the abandoning concurrent use applicant, the proceeding will be dissolved as to that applicant, and registration to that applicant will be refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the abandoning applicant reserves its rights to continue using the mark and is a specified excepted user in another involved application, the abandoning applicant remains a party as a common law concurrent user despite judgment being entered. Other applicants that listed the abandoning applicant as an excepted user still retain the burden of proving entitlement in view of the acknowledged rights of the abandoning applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of adverse decision in opposition or cancellation on concurrent use
rubrics_metrics.description: An adverse decision on priority in an opposition, cancellation, or interference proceeding does not necessarily preclude seeking concurrent use registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party may seek a concurrent use registration by filing a new application seeking concurrent use with the prevailing party before the Board, unless the party's first use in commerce was subsequent to the earliest application filing date of any conflicting application or registration owned by another party to the prior proceeding and that other party does not consent to a concurrent registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion (termination) of opposition or cancellation to concurrent use proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain conditions an opposition or cancellation may be terminated (often dismissed without prejudice) in favor of instituting a concurrent use proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situations permitting termination in favor of concurrent use include: (1) opposition filed by a party already specified in the application as an exception; (2) opposer files its own concurrent use application naming applicant as an exception and the opposer's application is published (and not opposed); (3) applicant amends its application to add opposer as an excepted user; (4) applicant files a motion to amend an unrestricted application to a concurrent use application reciting opposer as exception and opposer consents (or applicant consents to entry of judgment on unrestricted rights and amendment is approved). The opposition is typically suspended until publication/opposition resolution where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alteration of restrictions on concurrent registration
rubrics_metrics.description: A concurrent registration may be issued only pursuant to the decision of the Board in a concurrent use proceeding, or on the basis of a final court determination that multiple persons are entitled to use the same or similar marks in commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A registration cannot be territorially restricted by amendment under Trademark Act § 7(e), 15 U.S.C. § 1057(e), and 37 C.F.R. § 2.173(a). Alterations or restrictions must follow proper Board or court proceedings.
